title: Intune Compliance Policies and Configuration Baselines
summary: This lesson builds the device-trust foundation that the rest of Module 2 depends on. You will enroll devices into Microsoft Intune, then author compliance policies that evaluate OS version, BitLocker/disk encryption, firewall state, Defender real-time protection, and the device threat level reported by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. You will then push hardened configuration profiles and security baselines from the settings catalog to actively enforce BitLocker, Microsoft Defender Firewall, and Attack Surface Reduction. Finally you will see how the resulting compliant/noncompliant state becomes a first-class signal for Conditional Access, complete with 'mark device noncompliant' actions and grace periods.
objectives: Compare device enrollment models (Windows Autopilot, Automatic Enrollment, BYOD/MAM) and pick the right one per scenario.
Author an Intune compliance policy that checks OS version, BitLocker, firewall, Defender real-time protection, and device threat level.
Deploy configuration profiles and a settings-catalog security baseline that enforce BitLocker, firewall, and ASR.
Configure compliance actions for noncompliance, including 'mark device noncompliant' with a grace period and end-user notifications.
Explain how compliance state flows into Conditional Access as the 'require compliant device' grant control.
Validate compliance and configuration results from the Intune admin center and on the endpoint.

quiz.q: Which Intune compliance setting turns a Defender for Endpoint machine-risk score into a pass/fail compliance result?
options: Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score (device threat level)
quiz.why: The 'Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score' setting maps the MDE-reported threat level (Clear/Low/Medium/High) onto compliance, which is the hinge for the automated isolation loop later in the module.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a configuration profile and a compliance policy in Intune?
options: They are the same feature with different names
A configuration profile enforces/sets settings on the device; a compliance policy only evaluates and reports a state
A compliance policy enforces settings; a configuration profile only reports
Configuration profiles only apply to iOS
quiz.why: Configuration profiles and security baselines actively push and enforce settings (e.g., turn BitLocker on). Compliance policies evaluate the device against rules and produce a compliant/noncompliant state used by Conditional Access.

quiz.q: A compliance policy's action for noncompliance is set to 'Mark device noncompliant' with a schedule of 1 day. What happens?
options: The device is given a one-day grace period before its state flips to noncompliant
The user is blocked from sign-in for one day
Nothing until an admin manually approves
quiz.why: Setting the schedule to 1 day creates a grace period: the device is treated as compliant for one day after first failing, giving the user time to remediate before the state flips and Conditional Access reacts.

quiz.q: Where in Intune would you most efficiently configure dozens of granular Windows hardening settings (firewall, ASR, BitLocker) from a single searchable surface?
quiz.why: The Settings Catalog exposes the full library of Windows CSP settings in one searchable place, and is the modern recommended way to build configuration profiles and security baselines.

quiz.q: For an unmanaged personal phone accessing only Outlook and Teams, which enrollment approach is most appropriate?
options: App protection policies / MAM without device enrollment
quiz.why: MAM (app protection policies) protects corporate data inside managed apps without enrolling or fully managing the personal device, which is the right fit for BYOD where you only need to govern app data.

quiz.q: In 2-4 sentences, explain why deploying a compliance policy alone does not actually block a noncompliant device from reaching corporate resources, and what you must add.
quiz.answer: A compliance policy only evaluates the device and stamps it compliant or noncompliant in Entra ID; by itself it changes nothing about access. To enforce access decisions you must pair it with a Conditional Access policy that uses the 'Require device to be marked as compliant' grant control. Only then does a noncompliant state actually block sign-in to apps like Exchange Online or SharePoint.

body_markdown:
## Why device trust comes first

Zero Trust says *never trust, always verify* — and one of the strongest things you can verify is the health of the device making the request. In Microsoft Intune you build that verification in two halves: **configuration profiles / security baselines** that *enforce* a hardened state, and **compliance policies** that *evaluate* the device and stamp it compliant or noncompliant in Microsoft Entra ID. Conditional Access then consumes that stamp. Get this layer right and the automated isolation you build in Lesson 3 becomes almost free.

## Enrollment models: choose deliberately

Before a device can be governed it must be known to Intune. Pick the model that matches ownership and use case:

- **Windows Autopilot** — corporate Windows devices provisioned zero-touch from the OEM/reseller; the device joins Entra ID and enrolls automatically.
- **Automatic enrollment** — when a user Entra-joins a Windows device, MDM enrollment happens automatically (configured under *Devices > Enrollment*).
- **Hybrid Entra join** — on-prem AD-joined devices that also register in Entra; common in migration scenarios.
- **MAM / App protection (BYOD)** — personal phones where you protect *app data* (Outlook, Teams) without enrolling or fully managing the device.

Rule of thumb: full device management (and therefore compliance + configuration profiles) for corporate devices; MAM for unmanaged personal devices.

## Building a compliance policy

In the Intune admin center go to **Devices > Compliance > Create policy**, platform **Windows 10 and later**. Concrete settings to set:

- **Device Health**: Require BitLocker = *Require*; Require Secure Boot = *Require*; Code integrity = *Require*.
- **Device Properties**: Minimum OS version = e.g. `10.0.22631` (Windows 11 23H2 or later).
- **System Security**: Firewall = *Require*; Antivirus = *Require*; Microsoft Defender Antimalware real-time protection = *Require*; Encryption of data storage = *Require*.
- **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint**: *Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score* = **Medium**. This is the line that ties compliance to MDE's threat level — remember it for Lesson 3.

Assign the policy to a device or user group. A device that fails any rule will (after its action schedule) be marked noncompliant.

## Actions for noncompliance and grace periods

On the **Actions for noncompliance** tab you control the user experience and timing:

- **Mark device noncompliant** with *Schedule (days after noncompliance)* = `0` for immediate, or `1`–`3` to grant a **grace period** so users can self-remediate before access is cut.
- **Send email to end user** using a configured notification message template, optionally CC'ing the helpdesk.
- **Remotely lock** or **Retire the noncompliant device** for high-stakes scenarios.

Grace periods are a usability/security trade-off: too long and a risky device keeps access; `0` days gives the tightest containment, which is what you want for the threat-level rule.

## Enforcing settings with profiles and the settings catalog

Compliance *checks* but does not *fix*. Use **Devices > Configuration > Create > New policy > Settings catalog** to actively enforce. Search the catalog and add, for example:

- **BitLocker**: require encryption, XTS-AES 256, silent enablement, and escrow the recovery key to Entra ID.
- **Microsoft Defender Firewall**: enable Domain/Private/Public profiles, default inbound = block.
- **Attack Surface Reduction**: set ASR rules to *Block* (covered in depth in Lesson 2).

A simple way to read effective BitLocker state on an endpoint:

```powershell
# Confirm BitLocker is on and fully encrypted
Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: |
  Select-Object MountPoint, VolumeStatus, EncryptionPercentage, ProtectionStatus
```

## Security baselines as a fast hardening start

Instead of hand-picking hundreds of settings, deploy a **security baseline** (Devices > Security baselines) — Microsoft's recommended preconfigured set for Windows, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Microsoft Edge. Treat the baseline as your starting point, then layer targeted settings-catalog profiles for anything the baseline doesn't cover. Watch for **conflicts**: when two profiles set the same setting differently, Intune reports the device as *Conflict* and applies neither, so keep ownership of each setting clear.

## Closing the loop into Conditional Access

None of this blocks anything yet. Compliance state is just metadata until a **Conditional Access** policy uses it. In Entra create a policy targeting your users and cloud apps, and under *Grant* select **Require device to be marked as compliant**. Now a noncompliant Windows device is denied at sign-in to Exchange Online, SharePoint, and your SaaS apps. Validate end-to-end: break a rule (e.g., disable the firewall), confirm the device flips to noncompliant in *Devices > All devices*, and confirm sign-in is blocked. That round trip is exactly what you will automate in Lesson 3.

slides.title: Intune Compliance & Configuration Baselines
slides.sub: Building verifiable device trust for Zero Trust
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 2. In this first lesson we lay the foundation that everything else in modern endpoint security stands on: provable device trust. We will use Microsoft Intune to both enforce a hardened device state and evaluate it. By the end you will understand how a device's health becomes a signal that Conditional Access can act on.

slides.title: Enrollment models
bullets: Windows Autopilot: zero-touch corporate provisioning
Automatic enrollment on Entra join
Hybrid Entra join for migrating on-prem devices
MAM / app protection for BYOD without full management
slides.narration: A device must be known to Intune before you can govern it. Choose Autopilot or automatic enrollment for corporate Windows devices that you fully manage. For personal phones, MAM protects corporate data inside apps like Outlook and Teams without enrolling the whole device.

slides.title: Compliance policy: the rules
bullets: OS version floor, BitLocker, Secure Boot
Firewall on, antivirus + real-time protection on
Require device at or under MDE machine risk score
Evaluates state; does not enforce settings
slides.code:
# Compliance checks (conceptual)
Require BitLocker            = Require
Minimum OS version           = 10.0.22631
Firewall                     = Require
Defender real-time protection= Require
Machine risk score (MDE)     = Medium or lower
slides.narration: A compliance policy is a set of rules the device is measured against. Note the last rule: it ties compliance directly to the threat level reported by Defender for Endpoint. Keep that one in mind, because it is the hinge of the automated isolation loop two lessons from now.

slides.title: Actions for noncompliance
bullets: Mark device noncompliant (the key action)
Schedule in days = grace period (0 = immediate)
Email the end user from a template
Optional remote lock or retire
slides.narration: When a device fails a rule you decide what happens and how fast. The schedule field is a grace period in days, letting users self-remediate before access is cut. Set it to zero when you want the tightest possible containment, which is what we want for the threat-level rule.

slides.title: Enforce with the Settings Catalog
bullets: Configuration profiles set and enforce settings
Settings Catalog = one searchable surface for all CSPs
Enforce BitLocker, Defender Firewall, ASR
Escrow BitLocker recovery keys to Entra ID
slides.code:
Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: |
  Select-Object MountPoint, VolumeStatus,
    EncryptionPercentage, ProtectionStatus
slides.narration: Compliance checks but never fixes. Configuration profiles, built from the Settings Catalog, actively enforce the hardened state. Here we push BitLocker, the Defender firewall, and Attack Surface Reduction rules, and we make sure recovery keys are escrowed to Entra ID so users are never locked out.

slides.title: Security baselines
bullets: Microsoft's recommended preconfigured settings
Baselines for Windows, MDE, and Edge
Use as a starting point, then layer targeted profiles
Watch for conflicts: device shows 'Conflict', applies neither
slides.narration: Rather than hand-pick hundreds of settings, start from a Microsoft security baseline and layer your own targeted profiles on top. Just be deliberate about ownership: if two profiles set the same setting differently, Intune flags a conflict and applies neither.

slides.title: Compliance becomes a CA signal
bullets: Compliance state lives in Entra ID
Conditional Access grant: Require compliant device
Noncompliant = blocked from Exchange, SharePoint, SaaS
Validate by breaking a rule end to end
slides.narration: Compliance is just metadata until Conditional Access consumes it. With a 'require compliant device' grant control, a noncompliant Windows device is denied access to your apps at sign-in. Always validate the full round trip by deliberately breaking a rule and watching the block happen.

slides.title: Lab and recap
bullets: Enroll a Windows device and assign a baseline
Author the compliance policy with the MDE risk rule
Add a Conditional Access compliant-device policy
Break the firewall and confirm the block
slides.narration: In the lab you will stand up the full chain: enroll, harden with a baseline, evaluate with a compliance policy, and gate access with Conditional Access. This is the device-trust foundation. Next lesson we deepen the endpoint side by onboarding Defender for Endpoint and rolling out Attack Surface Reduction.
